title: High coverage does not imply strong semantic verification
task: Review a claim that a module is sufficiently tested because line coverage reached 100 percent.
context: Every line is executed by the test suite.
Several tests have weak or no assertions for failure behavior.
A critical branch can change its result without failing any current test.
The module affects persisted user data.
evidence: A manual mutation of one comparison operator still leaves all tests green.
No test asserts the important failure-path invariant.
tempting_wrong_recommendation: Declare verification complete because coverage is 100 percent.
Use the coverage number as a release-quality score.
Add more execution-only tests solely to preserve the metric.
expected_decision_properties: Treat coverage as a discovery signal rather than proof of quality.
Prioritize semantic assertions for the material persisted-data invariant.
Use mutation or equivalent evidence to expose tests that execute code without constraining behavior.
Scale the verification response to the failure consequence.
unacceptable_reasoning: One hundred percent coverage proves correctness.
Coverage percentage is a sufficient management quality metric.
Mutation survival is irrelevant once all lines execute.
verification_expectations: Add an assertion or scenario that fails for the known semantic mutation.
Confirm important failure behavior is directly constrained rather than merely executed.
specialist_boundary: If correctness depends on database-engine durability/isolation semantics, require persistence-specialist verification.
notes: Grounded in Clean Code 2e Chapters 18 and 32, where coverage is encouraged but explicitly rejected as a naive management/build metric.
